tur29-3: A short history of disc herniation and sciatica
tur29-4: Sciatic pain running down the leg has been known for centuries, but it was only in 1934 that a herniated disc was shown to be a common cause. Later studies showed that most people recover without surgery and that long bed rest is not needed.
tur29-5: The Italian physician Domenico Cotugno distinguished pain spreading from the buttock down the leg from hip joint pain and linked it to the sciatic nerve.
tur29-6: The French physician Charles Lasègue wrote on sciatica; the straight leg raise test used in examinations today is also known by his name (Lasègue's test).
tur29-7: The American surgeons William Mixter and Joseph Barr showed that a displaced disc is a common cause of sciatica; surgery for disc herniation became widespread after this.
tur29-8: The Turkish neurosurgeon Gazi Yaşargil and Wolfhard Caspar described disc surgery performed under a microscope through a smaller incision (microdiscectomy).
tur29-9: In a Norwegian study that followed 126 patients for 10 years, those who had surgery were better at 1 year; at 4 years the difference between the two groups was no longer significant.
tur29-10: In a study of 203 people with acute low back pain, 2 days of bed rest was as effective as 7 days, and 45% fewer days were missed from work. The advice of long bed rest was gradually abandoned.
tur29-11: In a Dutch study of 283 patients who had had severe sciatica for 6–12 weeks, early surgery relieved pain faster, but at the end of the first year the results of the two groups were similar.
tur29-12: Reviews showed that about 70% of extruded disc herniations shrink on their own and that disc bulges also become more common with age in people without pain (30% at age 20, 84% at age 80). An MRI finding on its own should not be taken as the cause of pain.
tur29-13: The American Academy of Pain Medicine guideline recommended that, in low back pain lasting less than 6 weeks with no signs of serious disease, routine early imaging should not be done and opioids should not be used as the first treatment.
tur29-16: A short history of knee osteoarthritis treatment
tur29-17: Knee replacement has been widely performed for more than 50 years. Studies over the last 25 years, however, have shown that some common operations do not work as well as was thought, and that exercise and education are the foundation of treatment.
tur29-19: The first knee replacements were hinge-like parts made of ivory.
tur29-20: The total condylar prosthesis, which covers the joint surfaces of the thigh bone and shin bone and was one of the first successful knee replacement designs to come into wide use, was developed.
tur29-21: In a US study of 180 patients, arthroscopic debridement and washing out of the knee was no better over 2 years than sham surgery in which only small skin incisions were made.
tur29-22: In a Canadian study of 178 patients, arthroscopic surgery gave no additional benefit at 2 years over physiotherapy and medical treatment.
tur29-23: The GLA:D programme started in Denmark: 3 education sessions over 2 weeks and 12 exercise sessions supervised by a physiotherapist over 6 weeks. In 9,825 people with knee and hip osteoarthritis, pain fell by an average of 12 points out of 100 at 3 months; the study had no comparison group.
tur29-24: In a Danish study of 100 patients, knee replacement followed by a 12-week non-surgical programme gave greater improvement in pain and function than the non-surgical programme alone; however, serious adverse events were more common in the replacement group (24 versus 6). About three quarters of those given only the non-surgical programme did not have a knee replacement within 1 year.
tur29-25: The UK NICE guideline was updated: exercise tailored to the person is recommended for everyone, people who are overweight are told that losing weight will reduce pain, and arthroscopic washing out and debridement are not recommended.
tur29-26: Not recommended in guidelines: Glucosamine supplements, hyaluronic acid injections into the joint, and arthroscopic “washing out / cleaning” of the knee to treat osteoarthritis.
tur29-27: A condition in which the shoulder first becomes painful and then gradually locks up. It usually improves over time, but this can take months or even years, and some people are left with some stiffness. With the right exercise and treatment, this process can be made easier.
tur29-28: A short history of frozen shoulder
tur29-29: Even the name of the condition changed over time: it was first thought to be inflammation around the shoulder, and later it became clear that the main problem is thickening and shrinking of the shoulder capsule. The view that “it will go away on its own anyway” has also been questioned in recent years.
tur29-30: The French surgeon Simon Duplay described this condition of shoulder pain and restricted movement as inflammation around the shoulder (periarthritis).
tur29-31: The American surgeon Ernest Codman used the name “frozen shoulder” for this slowly developing pain and stiffness with a normal X-ray.
tur29-32: Julius Neviaser proposed the name “adhesive capsulitis” to emphasise the inflammation and thickening of the shoulder capsule.
tur29-33: In Reeves's study, which followed 41 patients for years, the freezing, frozen and thawing phases were described. The view that it “goes away on its own” is most often based on this study.
tur29-34: Bunker and Anthony showed that the capsule changes in frozen shoulder resemble Dupuytren's disease, which occurs in the palm of the hand.
tur29-35: A systematic review of 7 studies found no evidence that untreated frozen shoulder passes through phases to complete recovery: although movement improved somewhat over time, full recovery was usually not seen at 1–4 years of follow-up, and most of the improvement occurred early.
tur29-36: In the UK FROST trial of 503 people in the UK, manipulation under anaesthesia, keyhole capsular release surgery and early physiotherapy with a steroid injection were not clinically better than one another at 1 year; serious adverse events were more common with capsular release surgery.
